strengths: Large-scale, geographically diverse dataset (83,137 annotated trees across 3 countries) addressing critical gap in tropical forest monitoring resources with open-access release
Rigorous experimental design with proper spatially-separated train/validation/test splits, comprehensive benchmarking of multiple architectures with detailed ablations
Practical RFI75 metric providing operationally meaningful evaluation that bridges pixel-level predictions to forest monitoring applications
Demonstrated benefit of multi-resolution training approach that improves generalization across spatial extents and GSDs without individual resolution trade-offs
Comprehensive generalization evaluation on 5 out-of-distribution datasets with clear performance comparisons and transparent methodology
Strong reproducibility through detailed hyperparameter documentation, open-source releases (models, libraries, benchmarking tools), and implementation details
Clear and well-organized presentation with appropriate balance of quantitative tables and qualitative visualizations throughout the paper
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty - paper is primarily a dataset and benchmarking contribution with no novel detection algorithms or architectural innovations

Annotation quality concerns inadequately addressed: incomplete/sparse annotations acknowledged but not quantified; single-pass annotation without secondary review; no inter-annotator agreement metrics or rater reliability statistics provided
Insufficient analysis of annotation completeness and how masking of missing annotations during training affects learning dynamics and introduces potential biases
RFI75 metric choice lacks justification: 75% IoU threshold appears arbitrary with limited sensitivity analysis; no comparison with alternative raster-level evaluation metrics
Limited ecological grounding: no validation against field ground truth measurements; unclear how detection errors propagate to downstream biodiversity/biomass estimation tasks
Insufficient analysis of forest type and tree structural diversity: limited quantitative assessment of representation across tropical forest types and canopy structures
Computational cost under-analyzed: missing inference cost requirements, memory footprint, and practical deployment considerations for field applications
Failure case analysis lacking: limited discussion of systematic failure modes, performance variation with tree size/crown shape/occlusion, or cases where methods consistently disagree
Statistical rigor gaps: no confidence intervals on key metrics, limited significance testing between method comparisons, no performance variance analysis across spatial regions
Multi-resolution training mechanism under-explored: limited analysis of why approach works (domain randomization vs. increased effective training size vs. invariance learning)

strengths: Large-scale, well-documented dataset with 83,137 labeled tree crowns across three tropical countries at high resolution (12 cm/pixel), addressing a critical gap in open-access forest monitoring data

Comprehensive and rigorous benchmarking across multiple architectures (Faster R-CNN, DeepForest, Detectree2, DINO) with proper spatial train/val/test splits and extensive out-of-distribution evaluation
Practical innovation: RFI_75 metric addresses real operational needs for raster-level forest monitoring performance assessment
Strong reproducibility efforts including released Python libraries (geodataset, CanopyRS), detailed hyperparameters, preprocessing documentation, and open-access dataset with CC-BY license
Effective demonstration that multi-resolution training improves generalization across architectures and spatial extents
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty for a top-tier AI conference: no new detection methods proposed, only benchmarking of existing architectures; multi-resolution training is straightforward data augmentation without deeper innovation

Severe out-of-distribution generalization failures: RF1_75 performance drops 50-60% on external datasets (from ~80% in-distribution to 30-40% OOD), raising fundamental questions about the dataset's practical utility and domain transferability

Annotation quality concerns inadequately addressed: single-pass annotation without secondary review, sparse annotations acknowledged but not quantified, no inter-annotator agreement statistics, and missing analysis of how annotation sparsity affects model training

Insufficient analysis and insights: no failure case investigation, missing explanations for key findings (e.g., why DINO dominates, what makes tropical detection fundamentally different, why certain forests are so difficult), no analysis of tree size distributions across countries

RFI_75 metric design lacks justification: 75% IoU threshold appears arbitrary, greedy matching algorithm is simplistic, large standard deviations (±0.15-0.45) for optimal thresholds indicate instability

Missing characterization of dataset differences from ecological perspective: limited analysis of forest types, canopy structure, species diversity, and how these affect model learning and generalization

Hyperparameter selection methodology concerns: grid search on validation set for NMS thresholds risks overfitting, multi-resolution augmentation ranges appear arbitrary, limited ablation studies on key design choices

strengths: Large-scale, high-quality dataset addressing a critical gap in tropical forest monitoring - 85,137 manually labeled tree crowns across three countries with high-resolution imagery (1.2-5.1 cm/pixel)

Methodologically rigorous experimental design with proper spatial separation of train/val/test splits using AOIs to avoid autocorrelation, comprehensive ablation studies of resolution/extent/input size effects, and detailed hyperparameter documentation

Comprehensive benchmarking across multiple architectures (Faster R-CNN, DeepForest, RetinaNet, Detectree2, DINO) with both within-distribution and extensive out-of-distribution evaluation on 7 external datasets showing strong generalization
Practical forest inventory-relevant metric (RFI₇₅) addressing limitations of standard tile-level COCO metrics and enabling fair comparisons across resolutions
Excellent reproducibility through open-source release including preprocessed dataset, geodataset and CanopyRS Python libraries, code, and pre-trained weights with comprehensive documentation

Multi-resolution training approach demonstrating clear performance improvements through straightforward but effective crop augmentation strategy achieving competitive zero-shot performance on unseen tropical forests

Clear and well-structured presentation with excellent visualizations (Figure 1 showing data diversity, Figure 4 showing spatial splits, Figures 10-15 showing qualitative results on diverse forest types)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic and methodological novelty - paper is primarily a dataset/benchmark contribution with straightforward application of existing detection methods without architectural innovations or new training strategies

Annotation quality concerns: single-pass manual annotation without secondary review, no inter-rater reliability statistics, incomplete coverage in Brazil (40% of trees), and unclear annotation protocol for small crowns given extreme long-tail size distribution shown in Figure 2

Evaluation limitations: RFI₇₅ metric uses somewhat arbitrary 75% IoU threshold with limited justification; tile-level comparisons acknowledged as incomparable across different spatial extents (40×40m vs 80×80m) yet presented together; missing comparison with recent transformer variants beyond DINO

Incomplete multi-resolution training analysis - computational cost implications not discussed, architectural differences in multi-resolution suitability not explained, error bars in Figure 3 overlap significantly raising questions about statistical significance, and sensitivity to crop augmentation ranges ([36,88] and [30,100] pixels) not studied

Generalization claims need qualification - 'state-of-the-art' claim partially supported with only 7 OOD datasets including some with small test sets; performance degradation on datasets like BCI50ha (39.39 RFI₇₅) and Detectree2 (34.97 RFI₇₅) unexplained

Missing systematic failure analysis and error characterization - no size-stratified detection accuracy analysis despite extreme tree size variation (2-50m diameter shown in Figure 2), no precision-recall curves, no confusion matrices, and no instructive failure case analysis

Limited dataset diversity and completeness: only 3 geographic sites in Amazon/Mesoamerica (no Paleotropics), single temporal season, RGB-only spectral modality without NIR/multispectral options, and no discussion of class imbalance or ecological diversity representation

Methodological choices lack thorough justification: 80% black pixel masking threshold, specific tile overlap percentages (50% and 75%), incomplete annotation masking strategy not validated through ablation, and complex preprocessing pipeline with many interdependent hyperparameters

strengths: Large-scale high-quality dataset (83k annotations, 3× prior tropical datasets) with rigorous expert annotation protocol and quality control, addressing critical gap in tropical forest monitoring
Excellent reproducibility with complete open-source release of dataset, preprocessing library, training/inference code, and pre-trained models under permissive licenses
Novel practical RF175 raster-level evaluation metric properly addressing edge effects and duplicate detections for operational forest monitoring applications
Comprehensive experimental methodology with proper spatially-separated splits, multiple random seeds, and systematic ablations on resolution/spatial extent
Strong empirical results with DINO-Swin-L ranking first/second across diverse datasets and demonstrating effective multi-resolution training
Rigorous statistical analysis including distribution comparisons across datasets and proper error quantification
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: primarily dataset and benchmarking contribution applying existing architectures; multi-resolution augmentation is straightforward rather than novel

Insufficient annotation quality validation: no inter-annotator agreement statistics, variability in bounding box tightness acknowledged but unmeasured, sparse annotation masking not empirically validated
Concerning generalization within tropical forests: SELVABOX-only model shows 13.8% RF175 drop on OOD BCI50ha despite same geographic region, questioning robustness claims
RF175 metric justification lacks rigor: 75% IoU threshold chosen as 'balanced' without principled justification or comparison to alternatives; metric is practical but not scientifically novel
Incomplete analysis of multi-resolution mechanism: unclear why crop+resize improves generalization; could be simply strong augmentation; limited ablation on hyperparameter sensitivity
Limited failure mode analysis: no systematic breakdown by tree size, crown density, or forest type; qualitative results shown but insufficient error characterization

strengths: Addresses a significant gap in tropical forest remote sensing with 83k+ manually annotated crowns across multiple countries
Rigorous annotation protocol with domain experts, multi-pass QC, and careful handling of edge cases (1,284 person-hours)
Careful experimental design with spatially separated train/test splits avoiding geospatial autocorrelation
Comprehensive benchmarking across multiple architectures and datasets with in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluation
Excellent reproducibility: all code, data, and model weights released under permissive licenses
Practical RF175 metric that meaningfully addresses raster-level evaluation needs for forest monitoring applications
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: uses only existing architectures (Faster R-CNN, DINO); multi-resolution approach is standard cropping/resizing augmentation; RF175 metric is straightforward (F1 at raster-level with arbitrary 75% IoU threshold)

Evaluation metric concerns: 75% IoU choice lacks rigorous justification; making comparison difficult to other papers; Appendix E reveals concerning sensitivity to IoU thresholds and NMS hyperparameters, with unexplained performance peaks on some datasets

Experimental design issues: hyperparameter search limited to ~10 combinations; inconsistent hyperparameters across datasets (Table 11) confounds data effects with tuning effects; baselines (DeepForest, Detectree2) use default parameters rather than retuning; data leakage concern on Detectree2 (original splits unrecoverable)

Improvements are modest and inconsistent: often within standard deviation (e.g., +4% on BCI50ha in Table 4); marginal gains on non-tropical datasets (Table 5) suggest limited generalization despite claims; 'state-of-the-art' claims sometimes overstated

Limited dataset scope: only 3 neotropical locations across 14 orthomosaics (limited geographic diversity despite 'spanning three countries' framing); mostly 2023 data (temporal coverage poor); cannot assess temporal generalization; incomplete annotations masked rather than improved

Annotation quality not rigorously validated: no inter-annotator agreement metrics reported; DSM usage mentioned but not detailed; no ablation on annotation completeness impact; masking sparse regions creates training artifacts

Missing critical analyses: no failure case analysis; no tree-size dependent performance analysis; computational costs not reported; Figure 3 shows multi-resolution and single-resolution often indistinguishable, questioning significance of claimed benefits
For top-tier ML venues: insufficient methodological novelty, domain-specific scope limiting broader impact, evaluation reveals instabilities and arbitrary choices undermining confidence in claims

strengths: Large-scale, high-quality dataset representing order-of-magnitude improvement over prior tropical forest datasets (83k vs. ~27k max)
Rigorous and comprehensive benchmarking across multiple architectures with proper ablation studies on resolution/spatial extent
Well-motivated raster-level evaluation metric (RF₁₇₅) addressing practical operational needs overlooked by prior work
Excellent reproducibility: dataset, code, pre-trained models, and two Python libraries all released; extensive hyperparameter documentation
Careful experimental methodology with spatially separated splits, proper handling of incomplete annotations, and multi-seed evaluation
Clear practical value for environmental monitoring of tropical forests—an important real-world application
Strong generalization: models trained on SELVABOX achieve state-of-the-art or competitive results on both tropical and non-tropical OOD datasets
Transparent about limitations; appropriate ethical considerations; comprehensive related work positioning
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: no novel detection architectures; multi-resolution training is standard data augmentation, not a methodological advance
Annotation quality validated only through photo-interpretation; no field validation or inter-annotator agreement metrics despite relying on 5 annotators
Evaluation compromised on Detectree2 dataset due to inability to recover original train-test splits; OAM-TCD appears in both training and validation sets
RF₁₇₅ metric, while well-motivated, is non-standard and makes future comparisons harder; 75% IoU threshold is somewhat arbitrary (acknowledged by authors who defer RF₁₅₀:₉₅ to future work)
Masking strategy for incomplete annotations lacks ablation studies and deeper analysis of potential unintended learning biases
Limited analysis of why models trained on SELVABOX generalize well to non-tropical datasets beyond the straightforward multi-resolution augmentation
Missing recent baselines: no comparison with newer vision transformers or recent detectors (YOLO-v8, RTMDet); SAM mentioned but not evaluated
Geographic scope limited to neotropical regions; no systematic analysis of failure modes, failure types, or false positive patterns
